title: Geohash: turning locations into searchable strings

kcs.statement: A geohash interleaves longitude and latitude bisection bits and encodes them in base32, so points that share a longer prefix lie in the same, smaller cell.
Each extra geohash character adds 5 bits and shrinks the cell about 32×. A 6-character geohash is roughly 1.2 km × 0.6 km.

Nearby points can sit on opposite sides of a cell boundary and share no prefix. A radius search therefore picks a precision, queries every cell that intersects the search circle, and filters candidates by exact distance; the centre cell plus its 8 neighbours is enough only when those cells are at least as large as the radius at that latitude.

problem_ideas: Implement encode(lat, lon, precision) in pure Python and check it against a known geohash.
Predict the cell size for 5, 6 and 7 characters and pick one for a 1 km search.
Two cafés 50 m apart have geohashes with no common prefix. Explain why and fix the query.
Implement cells_covering(lat, lon, radius_m, precision) that returns every cell intersecting the circle, and show a 3 km radius at precision 6 needs more than 9 cells.
Store restaurants in a SQL table with a geohash column and an index, then write the prefix query plus the exact-distance filter.
Explain why geohash cells near the poles are distorted and how that changes the cells a fixed radius covers.
